Okay, everybody, a few tips for day one. First, money. When you eat in a restaurant, the price on the menu is not the final price. Tax comes later, and so does the tip. Around here, a tip of eighteen to twenty percent is normal. When you want to pay, ask for the check. In England they say the bill, but here it's the check. Second, the restroom. Nobody says toilet here. Just ask, could you tell me where the restroom is? And finally, if you're lost, don't panic. Ask a stranger, politely. Do you know if this train goes to Brooklyn? Most people are happy to help, even in New York.

I'll be honest. On my first day I didn't leave the hotel. I ordered room service, twice, because I was terrified of speaking. Ridiculous, I know. On the second day I made myself go out. At the bus stop, I asked a woman, very slowly, if she knew whether the bus went downtown. She smiled, said yes, and asked me where I was from. We struck up a conversation, and twenty minutes later I had a list of the best cafes in the city. What did I learn? You don't need perfect language to get by. You just need to give it a shot, especially on day two.

I've worked at the front desk for six years, and I hear the same questions every day. The most common one is where the nearest pharmacy or supermarket is. Then people ask if the subway is safe at night, and how much a taxi to the airport costs. And in January, almost everybody asks me whether it's always this cold. That one makes me laugh. The answer is yes. What makes a guest sound polite? Small things. When someone starts with could you tell me, or I was wondering if, and then says thank you, I want to help them even more. It's not about perfect English. It's about the way you ask.
